newsitem.title: USA: Hunt Manufacturing to restructure, see charge. [CORRECTED 10:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Hunt Manufacturing to restructure, see charge. [CORRECTED 10:25 GMT]

text.p: Hunt Manufacturing Co said Tuesday it planned to restructure, focusing on the three business areas of consumer products, presentation graphics and substrates, and it expected to take a $22 million to $25 million pretax charge in fiscal 1997 related to the move.

The company said the strategy and restructuring, which should be fully implemented by the end of 1997 or early in 1998, would result in 10 to 15 percent revenue growth and 15 to 20 percent earnings growth into the next century.

Hunt said it would divest assets not directly related to the plan, including its Bevis office furniture operation. (Corrects to add dropped word "not", to make clear assets not directly related to the plan to be divested).

"Although no decision has been reached, the company is currently considering the sale of its Bevis brand office furniture operation, and has received indications of interest from several potential purchasers of Bevis," the company said in a statement.

The divestiture of Bevis as well as previously-announced sales of Lit-Ning brand products and facilities and Hunt Data products, would reduce the company's revenues on an annualized basis by about $100 million, it said.
At Hunt's Statesville, N.C. manufacturing and distribution facilities, about 5,000 stock keeping units of slow-moving and "non-strategic" products would be eliminated, it said.
While the product rationalization was expected to reduce sales, it was also projected to reduce overall operating costs, improve margins at the plants and improve inventory turns, the company said.
The company also said it was restructuring its corporate administrative functions and reducing administrative staffing.

Hunt said it was decentralizing corporate functions by moving them into three profit centers, as well as outsourcing of activities like payroll and benefits administration. The move would lower costs, it said.
The company said potential gains from a sale of Bevis should approximately offset special restructuring charges.
"We believe this new strategy will restore the higher levels of growth, profitability and returns that we expect and our shareholders deserve," Chairman Donald Thompson said.
